tasks.title: Discover the executive problem
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shows you can translate executive frustration into an operational problem.

Steps:
- [ ] Spend 5 minutes reading the fictional brief in 02-PRD.md. Label every scenario assumption as fictional.
- [ ] Ask the ten discovery questions in 05-Interview.md aloud. Answer as the fictional CEO for 15 minutes.
- [ ] Draw the current email-to-follow-up workflow and mark two failure points.
- [ ] Write one outcome, a baseline-measurement method, three constraints, and five unresolved questions.
- [ ] Record a 60-second playback and check that it describes a business problem before naming tools.

Deliverable: discovery.md and a current-state workflow

Definition of done: One user, one painful workflow, one measurable outcome, assumptions and unanswered questions documented.

Evidence: Discovery notes; 60-second recording; workflow sketch

Interview questions: How do you handle a vague CEO request? What would you measure first?

Executive explanation: I first identify which decisions get delayed and what information is missing.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: accepting “build an AI assistant” as a requirement. Recovery: ask for the last real example and the consequence of delay.
tasks.definitionOfDone: One user, one painful workflow, one measurable outcome, assumptions and unanswered questions documented.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Discovery notes; 60-second recording; workflow sketch
tasks.interviewCompetency: How do you handle a vague CEO request? What would you measure first?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.1

tasks.title: Map future workflow, roles and risky actions
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Defines who can see information and who is allowed to act.

Steps:
- [ ] Map ingest, extract, validate, review, approve, execute, audit.
- [ ] List operator, approver, worker and model permissions using the PRD matrix.
- [ ] Classify read-only summaries, proposed actions and consequential writes.
- [ ] Choose mock create_task as the sole executable action; explicitly exclude outbound email and real calendar changes.
- [ ] Write user stories for daily briefing, source inspection, approval and recovery.

Deliverable: workflow.md and permission matrix

Definition of done: Every state has an owner; the model has no approval or execution authority.

Evidence: Future-state diagram; roles matrix; five user stories

Interview questions: Authentication versus authorization? Which actions need approval?

Executive explanation: The assistant prepares the work, while the executive keeps control of commitments.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: a UI button is the only control. Recovery: enforce the same rule in the server and worker.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Every state has an owner; the model has no approval or execution authority.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Future-state diagram; roles matrix; five user stories
tasks.interviewCompetency: Authentication versus authorization? Which actions need approval?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.2

tasks.title: Finalize the implementation-ready PRD
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Precise acceptance criteria reduce coding-agent rework.

Steps:
- [ ] Read 02-PRD.md and replace only explicitly marked business assumptions.
- [ ] Confirm required fields, null semantics, confidence rules and citation checks.
- [ ] Walk each acceptance criterion through a concrete input and expected output.
- [ ] Number requirements and link each to a planned fixture or test.
- [ ] Ask the coding agent in plan mode to find ambiguities without implementing; resolve the top three.

Deliverable: docs/PRD.md with requirement-to-test matrix

Definition of done: No unresolved question blocks the core; non-goals, failure states and acceptance tests are explicit.

Evidence: PRD revision; ambiguity review; traceability matrix

Interview questions: What makes a PRD executable? Functional versus nonfunctional requirements?

Executive explanation: This document turns the desired result into checks we can demonstrate.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: describing features without failure behavior. Recovery: add invalid, duplicate, unauthorized and timeout examples.
tasks.definitionOfDone: No unresolved question blocks the core; non-goals, failure states and acceptance tests are explicit.
tasks.requiredEvidence: PRD revision; ambiguity review; traceability matrix
tasks.interviewCompetency: What makes a PRD executable? Functional versus nonfunctional requirements?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.3

tasks.title: Design persistence and integration contracts
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Persistence makes approvals and retries reliable across process restarts.

Steps:
- [ ] Copy the entity list and contracts from 02-PRD.md.
- [ ] Write an initial SQL migration with foreign keys, unique event keys and job indexes.
- [ ] Define input and output Zod schemas, including nullable owners and deadlines.
- [ ] Trace duplicate ingest and concurrent approval through database transactions.
- [ ] Write five sample request/response pairs and decide UTC storage versus Manila display.

Deliverable: 001_init.sql; schemas.ts; contracts.md

Definition of done: Duplicate events cannot create new work; approval version and action hash are persisted.

Evidence: Migration; contract examples; duplicate sequence diagram

Interview questions: Why PostgreSQL? How do indexes and transactions help?

Executive explanation: The database records what happened and prevents us from repeating an action accidentally.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: an in-memory Set for deduplication. Recovery: use database uniqueness and test after restart.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Duplicate events cannot create new work; approval version and action hash are persisted.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Migration; contract examples; duplicate sequence diagram
tasks.interviewCompetency: Why PostgreSQL? How do indexes and transactions help?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.4

tasks.title: Draw architecture and write five ADRs
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Tests whether you can explain trade-offs rather than recite tools.

Steps:
- [ ] Draw the PRD architecture from memory, then compare it with the reference.
- [ ] Write ADRs 1, 2, 4, 6 and 9 from 04-Decisions-Theory.md in your own words.
- [ ] For each, include reversal conditions and a measurable cost or operational implication.
- [ ] Rehearse one 30-second executive answer and one two-minute technical answer.
- [ ] Ask a reviewer to challenge your deployment and queue choices.

Deliverable: Architecture diagram; five ADRs

Definition of done: Each ADR has context, alternatives, decision, benefits, risks and a reversal trigger.

Evidence: Diagram; ADR files; two recorded answers

Interview questions: Why Railway instead of Vercel? Why not microservices or n8n?

Executive explanation: We are choosing the smallest design that can recover safely and be handed over.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: “scalable” without a load target. Recovery: defend the 20-event demonstration workload first.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Each ADR has context, alternatives, decision, benefits, risks and a reversal trigger.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Diagram; ADR files; two recorded answers
tasks.interviewCompetency: Why Railway instead of Vercel? Why not microservices or n8n?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.5

tasks.title: Threat-model the trust boundaries
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shows you can treat AI as shared infrastructure with constrained authority.

Steps:
- [ ] List assets and trust boundaries: source text, model output, application, database and tools.
- [ ] Trace malicious instructions in email and poisoned tool descriptions.
- [ ] Record threat, control, residual risk and test for six cases.
- [ ] Separate secret access from the model process and define redacted logging.
- [ ] Add stale approval, cross-workspace access and unknown execution outcome tests.

Deliverable: threat-model.md

Definition of done: Six threats each have a code-level control and observable negative test.

Evidence: Threat table; trust-boundary diagram; abuse cases

Interview questions: Can prompt injection be solved with a system prompt? What is tool poisoning?

Executive explanation: Incoming messages are evidence to analyze, never authority to change the system.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: relying on prompt wording as a security boundary. Recovery: remove tools and enforce permissions in code.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Six threats each have a code-level control and observable negative test.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Threat table; trust-boundary diagram; abuse cases
tasks.interviewCompetency: Can prompt injection be solved with a system prompt? What is tool poisoning?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.6

tasks.title: Create the repository, skeleton and CI
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Turns planning into an installable, testable starting point.

Steps:
- [ ] Follow setup commands in 03-Build-Labs.md in a new executive-ai-command-center folder.
- [ ] Check Node, Git, Claude Code and Docker availability; use hosted PostgreSQL if Docker is unavailable.
- [ ] Create src modules, package scripts, .env.example with names only, and .gitignore.
- [ ] Implement CLI help, health endpoint and a deterministic fake model adapter.
- [ ] Add one meaningful schema test and CI for install, typecheck, tests and build; commit the green skeleton.

Deliverable: Runnable skeleton and CI workflow

Definition of done: A fresh install prints CLI help; malformed input fails; CI commands pass locally.

Evidence: Commit hash; command transcript; CI link if a remote is configured

Interview questions: What belongs in CI? How do you make an app easy to install?

Executive explanation: We can now build on a repeatable foundation and detect mistakes early.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: spending this block on dashboard styling or OAuth. Recovery: keep CLI delivery and mock connectors.
tasks.definitionOfDone: A fresh install prints CLI help; malformed input fails; CI commands pass locally.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Commit hash; command transcript; CI link if a remote is configured
tasks.interviewCompetency: What belongs in CI? How do you make an app easy to install?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.7

tasks.title: Run the Day 1 gate and explanation drill
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Ensures you understand the design before delegating implementation.

Steps:
- [ ] Check PRD, contracts, migration, architecture, threat model and green skeleton.
- [ ] Explain one request end to end without reading notes.
- [ ] Answer three Day 1 interview questions using decision, reason, risk and evidence.
- [ ] Write the next handoff in progress.md and list missing evidence.
- [ ] Stop adding scope; reserve the next day for controlled implementation.

Deliverable: Day 1 evidence index and handoff

Definition of done: You can explain the flow in three minutes and name the largest remaining risk.

Evidence: Review checklist; recording; progress.md

Interview questions: Where is the main failure boundary? What would you cut first?

Executive explanation: The scope is clear, the risks are visible, and the first build has a passing check.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: treating generated documents as understanding. Recovery: redraw and explain with the documents closed.
tasks.definitionOfDone: You can explain the flow in three minutes and name the largest remaining risk.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Review checklist; recording; progress.md
tasks.interviewCompetency: Where is the main failure boundary? What would you cut first?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D1.8

tasks.title: Configure CLAUDE.md and plan mode
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Good context improves consistency without giving the agent unlimited freedom.

Steps:
- [ ] Record claude --version and claude --help; do not assume the CLI found in another shell is installed here.
- [ ] Copy the project instruction template in 03-Build-Labs.md.
- [ ] Start claude --permission-mode plan and request a plan for only ingestion and schema validation.
- [ ] Review files, tests, risks and acceptance criteria before allowing edits.
- [ ] Use /context and /memory to inspect what is loaded; save a short handoff before clearing context.

Deliverable: CLAUDE.md; implementation plan; version record

Definition of done: Agent identifies the scope and stops at the agreed plan without changing application code.

Evidence: Version output; plan; context screenshot

Interview questions: What belongs in CLAUDE.md? Is plan mode an authorization boundary?

Executive explanation: I give the coding assistant a clear brief and review the approach before implementation.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: a giant instruction file or hidden contradictory rules. Recovery: keep rules short and move procedures into a skill.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Agent identifies the scope and stops at the agreed plan without changing application code.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Version output; plan; context screenshot
tasks.interviewCompetency: What belongs in CLAUDE.md? Is plan mode an authorization boundary?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.1

tasks.title: Create and evaluate a project skill
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Makes repeated review work consistent and inspectable.

Steps:
- [ ] Create .claude/skills/review-contract/SKILL.md using the supplied template.
- [ ] Invoke /review-contract against the ingestion contract.
- [ ] Give it a deliberately incomplete contract and confirm it finds null, error and idempotency gaps.
- [ ] Check installed-version help for legacy .claude/commands support; use a skill as the primary slash command.
- [ ] Record what the skill improves, what it misses and how you would maintain it.

Deliverable: Project review skill and two evaluation examples

Definition of done: The skill identifies at least three planted gaps and does not edit files.

Evidence: SKILL.md; good/bad contract outputs

Interview questions: Skill versus command versus subagent? How do you evaluate a skill?

Executive explanation: This is a reusable review procedure so important checks are not forgotten.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: treating a downloaded skill as trusted policy. Recovery: review its source, dependencies and requested access first.
tasks.definitionOfDone: The skill identifies at least three planted gaps and does not edit files.
tasks.requiredEvidence: SKILL.md; good/bad contract outputs
tasks.interviewCompetency: Skill versus command versus subagent? How do you evaluate a skill?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.2

tasks.title: Add and test deterministic hooks
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Separates repeatable checks from model judgment.

Steps:
- [ ] Add the supplied PostToolUse validation hook in project settings.
- [ ] Use a dummy TypeScript edit that fails typechecking, then fix it and observe the hook result.
- [ ] Add a narrow PreToolUse deny for a fake protected fixture path, using documented hook output.
- [ ] Prove the deny with a harmless attempted edit; do not test on real secrets.
- [ ] Explain that hooks execute with local permissions and CI remains the release gate.

Deliverable: Hook configuration; validation log; protected-path test

Definition of done: Valid edit passes, invalid edit is reported, and protected fake path is unchanged.

Evidence: Settings diff; hook output; before/after file hash

Interview questions: PreToolUse versus PostToolUse? Why can hooks themselves be risky?

Executive explanation: Routine checks run every time instead of depending on the assistant remembering them.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: unsafe shell interpolation of tool arguments. Recovery: parse JSON and invoke fixed commands without a shell.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Valid edit passes, invalid edit is reported, and protected fake path is unchanged.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Settings diff; hook output; before/after file hash
tasks.interviewCompetency: PreToolUse versus PostToolUse? Why can hooks themselves be risky?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.3

tasks.title: Create five restricted development roles
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Demonstrates useful separation of implementation and independent review.

Steps:
- [ ] Create five .claude/agents files from the role specifications in 03-Build-Labs.md.
- [ ] Invoke each explicitly on its bounded assignment, sequentially first.
- [ ] Verify analyst/security/release roles lack write and shell tools.
- [ ] Give the security reviewer a fixture with a planted bypass and ask for evidence-backed findings.
- [ ] Score each role for correctness, scope adherence, evidence and cost; retain only roles that help.

Deliverable: Five role definitions and scored trial outputs

Definition of done: All five invoked; reviewers cannot edit; the planted bypass is reported.

Evidence: Agent files; invocation transcript; scorecard

Interview questions: Why use a separate reviewer? When are five agents too many?

Executive explanation: The builder and reviewer have different responsibilities, with access limited to their work.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: spawning every role for every task. Recovery: invoke roles only when separation adds independent evidence.
tasks.definitionOfDone: All five invoked; reviewers cannot edit; the planted bypass is reported.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Agent files; invocation transcript; scorecard
tasks.interviewCompetency: Why use a separate reviewer? When are five agents too many?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.4

tasks.title: Practice isolation, background work and handoffs
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shows you can coordinate AI-assisted changes without losing control of the repository.

Steps:
- [ ] Commit the baseline and create an explicit Git worktree for ingestion.
- [ ] Have implementation engineer implement only ingestion and its unit tests.
- [ ] Run a read-only security review in the background while you inspect the contracts in the main session.
- [ ] Collect its result; compare changed files with the assigned scope and rerun tests.
- [ ] Save a concise handoff and resume in a fresh session; review and integrate only the intended commit.

Deliverable: Ingestion commit; worktree and handoff evidence

Definition of done: No unrelated diff; tests pass; fresh session explains the state accurately.

Evidence: git diff; test result; review findings; progress.md

Interview questions: What does a worktree isolate? What does it not isolate?

Executive explanation: Independent work stays separate until it has been reviewed and tested.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: assuming worktrees isolate databases or credentials. Recovery: separate test database names and use mock secrets.
tasks.definitionOfDone: No unrelated diff; tests pass; fresh session explains the state accurately.
tasks.requiredEvidence: git diff; test result; review findings; progress.md
tasks.interviewCompetency: What does a worktree isolate? What does it not isolate?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.5

tasks.title: Review and connect one local mock MCP server
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shows protocol understanding without wasting time on production OAuth.

Steps:
- [ ] Use the in-process mock memory tool from the SDK lab; for Claude Code wrap the same read function in a reviewed stdio server.
- [ ] Record repository origin, exact version or commit, tools, permissions and network destinations.
- [ ] Configure the local server with claude mcp add using the exact local script path.
- [ ] Use /mcp and call one read-only mock lookup; deny or omit write capabilities.
- [ ] Return an unavailable error and a malicious instruction in fixture data; verify controlled handling.

Deliverable: MCP configuration; provenance record; three tool traces

Definition of done: Read works; unavailable is explicit; malicious content triggers no unauthorized action.

Evidence: Redacted config; source commit; traces

Interview questions: MCP host/client/server? Why prefer direct API for one connector?

Executive explanation: We test the connector with limited access before trusting it with company information.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: unpinned npx downloads with broad credentials. Recovery: inspect and pin locally, then connect only needed tools.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Read works; unavailable is explicit; malicious content triggers no unauthorized action.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Redacted config; source commit; traces
tasks.interviewCompetency: MCP host/client/server? Why prefer direct API for one connector?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.6

tasks.title: Run one bounded Ralph-loop experiment
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Lets you discuss persistence based on a measured experiment.

Steps:
- [ ] Read the official Ralph plugin source, pin the reviewed revision and confirm compatibility.
- [ ] Use a disposable worktree and fake inputs; target a single pure normalization function with three fixed tests.
- [ ] Run /ralph-loop with max-iterations 3 and a completion promise tied to the tests.
- [ ] Set an external 15-minute timer, review cost after every iteration, and cancel on repeated identical failure.
- [ ] Compare one normal agent attempt against the loop: tests passed, diff, time, cost and failure modes.

Deliverable: Bounded loop trial and ADRs 7, 8, 10

Definition of done: Loop stops on success, max iterations or manual cancel; no real integrations are available.

Evidence: Prompt; iteration log; diff; cost; ADRs

Interview questions: Ralph loop versus subagents? Why is a completion promise not a test?

Executive explanation: A bounded retry loop can finish repetitive work, but it must have an objective test and stop conditions.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: default unlimited iterations or changing tests to force success. Recovery: cap iterations and freeze the test oracle.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Loop stops on success, max iterations or manual cancel; no real integrations are available.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Prompt; iteration log; diff; cost; ADRs
tasks.interviewCompetency: Ralph loop versus subagents? Why is a completion promise not a test?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.7

tasks.title: Test recent releases and defend orchestration
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Proves that you test releases instead of repeating announcements.

Steps:
- [ ] Follow the four short experiments in 06-Frontier.md, within the shared 60-minute budget.
- [ ] Capture versions, exact release dates, source links and actual results.
- [ ] For unavailable API access record blocked, the exact requirement, and the fallback; do not fabricate a run.
- [ ] Write ADRs 3 and 5 and finish any remaining orchestration rationale.
- [ ] Give a two-minute explanation of why the production app still uses one extraction agent.

Deliverable: Release experiment log; remaining ADRs

Definition of done: Each selected release has a dated source and worked/failed/use-it record; unrun experiments are labeled.

Evidence: Versioned experiment logs; ADRs; recording

Interview questions: What changed recently? What did you test yourself?

Executive explanation: I adopt a new feature only after checking whether it improves a real task.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: calling roadmap items shipped features. Recovery: require a dated release entry and a reproducible observation.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Each selected release has a dated source and worked/failed/use-it record; unrun experiments are labeled.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Versioned experiment logs; ADRs; recording
tasks.interviewCompetency: What changed recently? What did you test yourself?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D2.8

tasks.title: Wire the Agent SDK with safe tools and limits
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Distinguishes an application agent from an interactive coding assistant.

Steps:
- [ ] Install and pin the SDK version reviewed in 06-Frontier.md.
- [ ] Implement the SDK adapter in 03-Build-Labs.md with tools: [], only read-only memory MCP and structured output.
- [ ] Set model through config, maxTurns 6, maxBudgetUsd 0.25 and a 60-second AbortController.
- [ ] Handle non-success result subtypes and exceptions as failed jobs, not empty successes.
- [ ] Run one live synthetic fixture if an API key is configured; otherwise prove fake mode and label live integration blocked.

Deliverable: agent.ts adapter; configuration validation

Definition of done: One valid typed output or explicit failure; no shell, write or execution tool is exposed.

Evidence: Package lock; redacted run; turns, tokens and cost

Interview questions: Agent SDK versus Messages SDK? Does allowedTools restrict all tools?

Executive explanation: The model has a small job, limited tools and a budget, so its behavior is easier to control.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: assuming allowedTools is an exclusive allowlist. Recovery: remove built-ins with tools: [] and register only safe tools.
tasks.definitionOfDone: One valid typed output or explicit failure; no shell, write or execution tool is exposed.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Package lock; redacted run; turns, tokens and cost
tasks.interviewCompetency: Agent SDK versus Messages SDK? Does allowedTools restrict all tools?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D3.1

tasks.title: Implement extraction, citations and escalation
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Trust depends on showing where claims came from and exposing uncertainty.

Steps:
- [ ] Extract five claim kinds using the PRD schema.
- [ ] Validate output with Zod and independently check source IDs and exact quote containment.
- [ ] Use null for missing owners/deadlines; preserve relative date text and normalize only with a known anchor.
- [ ] Apply deterministic confidence downgrade rules for missing or conflicting evidence.
- [ ] Build the daily briefing as a deterministic view of validated claims, with coverage and warning flags.

Deliverable: Extractor, citation validator and briefing command

Definition of done: Every displayed claim links to a valid source; ambiguous claims enter review.

Evidence: Input/output pairs; invalid-citation test; briefing sample

Interview questions: Structured output versus factual accuracy? Can confidence be treated as probability?

Executive explanation: Every claim shows its source, and unclear information stays visibly unresolved.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: another freeform summary invents uncited facts. Recovery: compose the briefing only from validated claims.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Every displayed claim links to a valid source; ambiguous claims enter review.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Input/output pairs; invalid-citation test; briefing sample
tasks.interviewCompetency: Structured output versus factual accuracy? Can confidence be treated as probability?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D3.2

tasks.title: Persist jobs, checkpoints and organizational memory
tasks.description:
Why it matters: The system must recover without depending on one model conversation.

Steps:
- [ ] Apply the migration to a development database and seed one workspace.
- [ ] Write ingest-and-enqueue in one transaction; claim jobs with leases and bounded retries.
- [ ] Persist job stages and optionally SDK session ID; never use session history as the business database.
- [ ] Add approved memory facts with source, version and supersedes relationship.
- [ ] Kill and restart the worker mid-job; replay safely and show an earlier confirmed preference used in a new briefing.

Deliverable: Database-backed worker and memory lookup

Definition of done: Restart preserves approved facts and job state; no duplicate committed extraction.

Evidence: Restart trace; database rows; memory citation

Interview questions: Session versus durable business state? Long context versus retrieval?

Executive explanation: The system remembers verified business facts and can recover when a process stops.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: saving unreviewed model summaries as truth. Recovery: make memory promotion a reviewed transition with provenance.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Restart preserves approved facts and job state; no duplicate committed extraction.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Restart trace; database rows; memory citation
tasks.interviewCompetency: Session versus durable business state? Long context versus retrieval?
tasks.notes: Fictional/synthetic executive data only. Full instructions: 01-Sprint-Workbook.md, task D3.3

tasks.title: Build the approval gate and immutable audit events
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Consequential actions must be tied to what a person actually approved.

Steps:
- [ ] Create proposed actions with canonical payload hashes and versions.
- [ ] Implement approve/reject authorization in the application, with expiry and optimistic concurrency.
- [ ] Write approval, job enqueue and audit event in the same transaction.
- [ ] Reject changed payloads and stale decisions; approval must never be inferred from source text.
- [ ] Run tests for unauthorized approval, double-click and payload mutation.

Deliverable: Approval commands and audit records

Definition of done: Only an authorized human can approve the exact action version; mutation invalidates approval.

Evidence: Approval screenshots or CLI transcript; three negative tests

Interview questions: How do you prevent approval time-of-check/time-of-use bugs?

Executive explanation: Approval applies to the exact action you reviewed, and we record who approved it.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: allowing the model to set approved=true. Recovery: exclude approval fields from model outputs and enforce server transitions.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Only an authorized human can approve the exact action version; mutation invalidates approval.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Approval screenshots or CLI transcript; three negative tests

tasks.title: Execute safely with retries and idempotency
tasks.description:
Why it matters: This is where an impressive demo becomes a defensible system.

Steps:
- [ ] Implement only mock create_task with a unique action-version idempotency key.
- [ ] Recheck approval, payload hash and expiry immediately before execution.
- [ ] Use 5-second tool timeout, at most 3 attempts and exponential backoff with jitter.
- [ ] Classify 429/5xx, permanent 4xx and uncertain side-effect outcomes differently.
- [ ] Test two workers, duplicate job delivery and a crash after the provider applied an action.

Deliverable: Executor and fake provider with fault injection

Definition of done: Exactly one mock side effect under concurrent retries; uncertain real-provider outcome would require reconciliation.

Evidence: Concurrency test; retry trace; effect count; audit trail

Interview questions: Can you guarantee exactly-once delivery? When should you not retry?

Executive explanation: We retry temporary failures without creating repeated commitments.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: replaying all errors blindly. Recovery: distinguish retryable, permanent and unknown-outcome states.
tasks.definitionOfDone: Exactly one mock side effect under concurrent retries; uncertain real-provider outcome would require reconciliation.

tasks.title: Run 20 golden and failure evaluation fixtures
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Interview claims need repeatable evidence, including negative cases.

Steps:
- [ ] Load the 20 fixtures in 07-evaluation-fixtures.json.
- [ ] Run deterministic unit/integration checks first, then live extraction cases within the approved budget.
- [ ] Score schema validity, citation validity, precision/recall, abstention, latency and cost separately.
- [ ] Run adversarial fixtures and assert zero unauthorized or duplicate effects.
- [ ] Record fixture version, model, prompt hash, commit and failures; fix the highest-impact defect and rerun affected cases.

Deliverable: Evaluation report with denominator and measured results

Definition of done: All deterministic safety cases pass; extraction meets PRD gates or limitations are clearly documented.

Evidence: Raw redacted results; score table; failing and fixed examples

Interview questions: What is a golden dataset? How do you prevent evaluation overfitting?

Executive explanation: We test the assistant against examples with known answers and deliberate failures.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: claiming 100% accuracy from 20 cases. Recovery: state the small sample and separate safety checks from quality metrics.
tasks.definitionOfDone: All deterministic safety cases pass; extraction meets PRD gates or limitations are clearly documented.
tasks.requiredEvidence: Raw redacted results; score table; failing and fixed examples

tasks.title: Complete the user workflow and handoff path
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Another person must be able to operate the software without you narrating every step.

Steps:
- [ ] Implement the documented CLI commands for ingest, briefing, sources, approvals, audit and retry.
- [ ] Add clear help, actionable errors and a sample-data reset limited to the demo workspace.
- [ ] Expose authenticated API routes only if deploying the service; keep a public health response nonsensitive.
- [ ] Spend at most 20 minutes on a read-only briefing HTML view if the CLI gate already passes.
- [ ] Ask a second person to follow the README, or perform a clean-room self-test from a new folder.

Deliverable: Complete CLI workflow; optional briefing view

Definition of done: A fresh operator can ingest fixtures, inspect citations and approve one mock action from written steps.

Evidence: Clean-room transcript; usability notes; corrected README

Interview questions: How do you package software for someone else? What do you cut to ship?

Executive explanation: A useful handover means the next person can run and troubleshoot the workflow.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: adding Next.js before reliable execution works. Recovery: ship the documented CLI first and label the UI as optional.

tasks.title: Run the end-to-end build gate
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Checks that the components work together, not just in isolation.

Steps:
- [ ] Run ingest to briefing to approval to execution to audit.
- [ ] Replay the same event and approved action; confirm stable counts.
- [ ] Restart the worker and repeat the read path.
- [ ] Record a three-minute walkthrough with one failure demonstration.
- [ ] Freeze scope and write the remaining release risks.

Deliverable: Release-candidate commit and evidence index

Definition of done: Happy path plus duplicate, unauthorized and recovery paths are demonstrable.

Evidence: Commit; recording; test report; limitations

Interview questions: Where can partial failure occur? What is your release blocker?

Executive explanation: The core workflow works end to end, including the cases where something goes wrong.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: demonstrating only the happy path. Recovery: rehearse a duplicate request and failed tool before the final demo.

tasks.title: Audit provenance, permissions and dependencies
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shared infrastructure needs an accountable supply chain and limited access.

Steps:
- [ ] Review MCP server, plugin and skill source origins, pinned versions, maintainers and install scripts.
- [ ] Compare tool descriptions and capabilities against the reviewed baseline to detect rug pulls.
- [ ] Inspect npm dependency changes and advisory findings; document triage rather than counting alerts.
- [ ] Map hypothetical Gmail/Slack/Calendar scopes to exact read operations; keep real OAuth outside the sprint.
- [ ] Repeat injection, role-boundary and redacted-logging tests.

Deliverable: Security review with evidence and residual risks

Definition of done: No unresolved critical bypass; every external component has a reviewed source and pinned revision.

Evidence: Provenance inventory; lockfile; scope matrix; negative tests

Interview questions: How do you assess a third-party MCP? OAuth versus OIDC?

Executive explanation: We check who built each extension, what it can access, and what changed before adopting it.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: trusting an official-looking name or readOnlyHint. Recovery: verify publisher and enforce permissions independently.
tasks.definitionOfDone: No unresolved critical bypass; every external component has a reviewed source and pinned revision.

tasks.title: Package the application and operator guide
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Your trial is stronger when another person can install it consistently.

Steps:
- [ ] Complete README prerequisites, install, configuration names, migration, seed and demo commands.
- [ ] Create a non-root Docker image and docker-compose configuration where Docker is available.
- [ ] Keep API keys out of image layers and logs; document injection through runtime configuration.
- [ ] Write troubleshooting entries for auth, DB, quota, missing model, stuck job and citation failure.
- [ ] Run install and fake-mode demo from a fresh directory.

Deliverable: README, Dockerfile, .env.example and troubleshooting guide

Definition of done: Instructions work without undocumented steps; fake mode does not require an API key.

Evidence: Clean install transcript; image tag; operator checklist

Interview questions: What makes a good handoff? How do you separate demo and production settings?

Executive explanation: The package includes a repeatable install path and clear answers for common problems.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: relying on global tools or a personal home directory. Recovery: declare versions and use project scripts.

tasks.title: Deploy a private demonstration service
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Shows you understand runtime constraints and can defend the hosting choice.

Steps:
- [ ] Use the release checklist in 08-Operations-Demo.md to deploy the pinned container on Railway if account and budget allow.
- [ ] Configure database and API key via host secrets, with separate operator and approver credentials.
- [ ] Bind the server to the host port and all interfaces; keep model execution in the worker.
- [ ] Run migration, seed synthetic data and verify health, authentication and one end-to-end run.
- [ ] Record actual plan/cost constraints; if paid hosting is unavailable, validate the local container and mark cloud deployment blocked.

Deliverable: Private deployment URL or explicitly labeled local release

Definition of done: No anonymous access to briefing or mutation routes; exact release commit and health evidence recorded.

Evidence: Deployment log; private URL; smoke test; cost estimate

Interview questions: Why Railway? What is a Vercel function runtime limitation?

Executive explanation: The demo is deployed where its worker can run reliably, with access limited to authorized users.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: assuming free hosting or exposing an unauthenticated dashboard. Recovery: verify current plan and keep local delivery if access is unavailable.

tasks.title: Rehearse monitoring, recovery and rollback
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Connects your production-support experience to application ownership.

Steps:
- [ ] Track queue age, failures, denied actions, latency and cost without message bodies in normal logs.
- [ ] Simulate model outage and stale worker lease; record incident timeline and recovery.
- [ ] Export a demo database backup and restore it into a separate empty database.
- [ ] Redeploy the previous application image against a compatible schema; document forward-fix for destructive migrations.
- [ ] Write owner, severity, communication cadence, RPO/RTO targets and measured drill results.

Deliverable: Operations runbook and recovery drill

Definition of done: One restore and one rollback path demonstrated, or precisely labeled blocked with reason.

Evidence: Sanitized incident timeline; restore counts; rollback smoke test

Interview questions: Health check versus monitoring? What would you do during a production incident?

Executive explanation: We know how to notice a failure, contain it and restore service without repeating actions.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: having a backup without testing restore. Recovery: restore to a separate database and compare known records.

tasks.title: Record the five-minute demo and architecture tour
tasks.description:
Why it matters: An executive needs to understand the benefit and the control model quickly.

Steps:
- [ ] Follow the minute-by-minute script in 08-Operations-Demo.md.
- [ ] Show one briefing with citations, an ambiguous claim, approval and the resulting audit event.
- [ ] Replay a duplicate request and show no extra side effect.
- [ ] Explain the architecture with the diagram and one ADR.
- [ ] Re-record once after removing jargon and disclose mock connectors and remaining limitations.

Definition of done: Demo stays within five minutes and includes evidence, control and failure behavior.

Evidence: Video; demo data; architecture slide or diagram

Interview questions: What would you show a CEO first? What is still missing for production?

Executive explanation: Here is the decision support, its evidence, and the point where you retain control.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: spending the demo on installation or tool lists. Recovery: pre-seed data and lead with the briefing.

tasks.title: Rehearse six truthful STAR stories
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Makes your infrastructure and automation experience relevant without inventing outcomes.

Steps:
- [ ] Use the six worksheets in 05-Interview.md.
- [ ] Fill missing DXC context, your exact responsibility, actions, outcomes and evidence.
- [ ] Keep unverified metrics out; distinguish portfolio claims from independently measured results.
- [ ] Record each answer in 90 seconds, emphasizing your personal decision and lesson.
- [ ] Ask a reviewer to probe what you personally did and what you would change.

Deliverable: Six STAR story cards with fact gaps resolved or marked

Definition of done: Each story has a true specific example, personal action, outcome and lesson.

Evidence: Story cards; source notes; recordings

Interview questions: Tell me about an incident, unclear requirement or risky change.

Executive explanation: My experience taught me to make changes carefully, explain risk and support the person using the system.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: claiming team outcomes as individual results. Recovery: distinguish “I did” from “the team achieved.”

tasks.title: Run technical and executive mock interviews
tasks.description:
Why it matters: Tests explanation under pressure and reveals the last high-value gaps.

Steps:
- [ ] Run a 35-minute technical interview using 05-Interview.md without opening notes.
- [ ] Run a 20-minute CEO conversation about vague priorities, cost and trust.
- [ ] Score accuracy, trade-offs, evidence, clarity and ownership from 0 to 2 each.
- [ ] Spend 15 minutes repairing the two weakest answers and 5 minutes repeating them.
- [ ] Prepare an honest answer about what you built personally, what AI helped with and what is still a prototype.

Deliverable: Mock interview scores and corrected answers

Definition of done: At least 8/10 on the final explanation rubric; no invented claims or hidden limitations.

Evidence: Recording; scored rubric; before/after answers

Interview questions: System design, debugging, prioritization, feedback, independence and support questions.

Executive explanation: I can explain the value, defend the choices and be clear about the remaining risks.

Common mistakes and recovery: Mistake: memorizing product terminology. Recovery: explain one observed failure and the code-level control that handled it.

- [ ] Build an evidence index linking PRD, commits, tests, ADRs, demo and runbook.
